answer.q: How does the engine of a car start?

els.title: title | Starting a car engine
els.spark: label 640 130 c=red s=24 | spark + fuel = bang!
els.done: label 250 515 c=blue s=26 | Now the engine runs itself, and the starter lets go

steps.say: When you turn the key or press start, you close an electric switch.
That lets the battery send a big burst of current to a small electric motor, called the starter.
The starter spins a heavy wheel, the flywheel, which turns the engine's crankshaft.
Now the pistons move, sucking in air and fuel and squeezing it tight.
A spark plug fires, the fuel explodes, and the blast pushes the piston down hard.
Each bang keeps the crankshaft turning, so the engine runs by itself and the starter switches off.

answer.q: How does a car's engine work?

els.title: title | Inside a car engine
els.note: label 560 515 c=blue s=24 | Thousands of bangs a minute!

steps.say: A car engine turns fuel into motion, using lots of tiny explosions.
First, the piston slides down and sucks fuel and air into the cylinder.
Then it moves back up and squeezes that mixture tight.
A spark plug lights it, and the bang shoves the piston down hard.
Finally the piston rises again and pushes the burnt gas out the exhaust.
The rod turns a crankshaft, and gears pass that spin to the wheels.
Suck, squeeze, bang, blow, thousands of times a minute, and the car rolls on.

els.title: title | Why is the sky blue?
els.tWhite: label 200 215 s=24 | white light = all colours
els.tR: label 320 410 c=red s=22 | red: long waves
els.tB: label 320 470 c=blue s=22 | blue: short waves
els.tRed: label 650 300 c=red s=22 | red mostly passes straight
els.tBlue: label 600 80 c=blue s=24 | blue bounces everywhere
els.tFinal: label 40 525 c=blue s=26 | Blue light reaches your eyes from every direction, so the whole sky glows blue!

steps.say: Sunlight looks white, but it is really a mix of every colour.
Each colour travels as a wave. Red waves are long, and blue waves are short and choppy.
The air is full of tiny gas molecules, much smaller than these waves.
do: fill m1 m2 m3 m4 m5

steps.say: Short blue waves hit them and scatter in every direction, much more than red.
The long red waves mostly slip straight through.
So wherever you look, scattered blue light is coming toward your eyes, and the whole sky glows blue.

els.title: title | How vaccines train your body
els.lblWeak: label 200 270 c=sky s=22 | Harmless piece of a germ
els.lblCell: label 380 395 s=22 | White blood cells study it
els.lblAb: label 560 470 c=blue s=22 | Antibodies made to fit it
els.memory: tag 480 115 270 44 f=#fff3c4 | Memory: I know this germ!
els.win: label 90 520 c=red s=26 | Caught fast, so you stay healthy!

steps.say: A vaccine is like a training session for your immune system.
It carries a harmless piece of a germ, or a weakened germ, that cannot make you sick.
Your white blood cells find it and study its shape.
Then your body builds antibodies, little Y-shaped tools made to fit exactly that germ.
Most importantly, memory cells remember the germ for years.
So if the real germ ever attacks, your body recognises it straight away and fights it off before you get sick.

els.title: title | The derivative: slope right now
els.sec: secant 40 90 420 330 f=x^2 at=1 h=2,1,0.5 | Secant lines get closer
els.tan: tangent 500 90 420 330 f=x^2 at=1 x=-1,3 y=-1,9 | Tangent at x = 1
els.q1: tag 250 470 380 44 f=#fff3c4 s=24 | Average speed between two points
els.q2: tag 710 470 380 44 f=#c8f7c5 s=24 | Speed at one instant
els.rule: text 250 525 s=26 | derivative = how fast something changes, right now

steps.say: A derivative tells you how fast something is changing at one exact moment.
Pick two points on a curve and join them. The slope of that line is the average rate of change.
Now slide the second point closer and closer. The line turns and settles into one position.
In the limit, it just touches the curve at one point. This is the tangent line.
The slope of the tangent is the derivative. For x squared at x equals one, it is two.
So a speedometer reading is a derivative: how fast your position changes, right now.

answer.q: How does a binary search work?

els.title: title | Binary search: halve and conquer
els.sorted: label 120 330 c=sky s=22 | sorted, smallest to largest
els.cmp1: label 140 400 c=red s=28 | 23 > 16, so throw away the left half
els.cmp2: label 140 400 c=red s=28 | 23 < 38, so throw away the right side
els.fnd: label 500 340 c=green s=26 | Found in 3 checks!
els.sum: label 140 470 c=blue s=28 | Each check halves the list: 1 million items take about 20 checks

steps.say: Binary search finds an item in a sorted list by cutting the list in half again and again.
do: fill c0 c1 c2 c3 c4 c5 c6 c7 c8

steps.say: Say we want to find twenty three. We start by looking at the middle item, sixteen.
Twenty three is bigger than sixteen, so it can't be anywhere on the left. We throw that whole half away.
Now we check the middle of what's left, which is thirty eight. That's too big, so we drop the right side.
Only one item is left, and it's twenty three. Found it in just three checks.
Every check halves the list, so even a million items take only about twenty checks.

answer.q: What is the difference between mitosis and meiosis?

els.title: title | Mitosis vs meiosis
els.nme: label 580 500 s=22 | 4 unique cells, half the set

steps.say: Mitosis and meiosis are the two ways a cell can divide.
In mitosis, one cell copies its forty six chromosomes, then splits in two.
The two new cells are identical copies, used to grow and repair your body.
Meiosis divides twice, making four cells, and halves the chromosomes to twenty three.
Each one is unique because the genes get shuffled. These become eggs or sperm.
So mitosis makes copies of you, and meiosis makes new mixes for the next generation.

els.title: title | Interest on interest
els.chart: moneygrow 350 90 570 350 p=100 r=10 n=10 cur=$ simple=1 | Compound vs simple
els.note: label 400 525 c=red s=22 | After 10 years: about $259, not $200

steps.say: Compound interest means you earn interest on your interest, not just on what you put in.
Say you save one hundred dollars at ten percent a year.
After one year the bank adds ten dollars, so you have one hundred and ten.
Next year, ten percent of one hundred and ten is eleven dollars. The interest earned interest too.
Each year the pile is bigger, so each year's interest is bigger, and the growth speeds up.
After ten years you'd have about two hundred fifty nine dollars, not two hundred. So start saving early!

answer.q: A patient weighs 70 kg. Heparin is ordered at 18 units/kg/hr, and the bag has 25,000 units in 250 mL. What rate in mL/hr?

els.title: title | Heparin drip rate
els.check: label 60 470 c=red s=20 | Check: 12.6 mL × 100 = 1260 units/hr ✓

steps.say: First, find the hourly dose. Multiply the weight by the ordered dose.
Seventy kilograms times eighteen units is 1260 units per hour.
Next, find the concentration: 25,000 units divided by 250 millilitres is 100 units per millilitre.
Now divide the dose by the concentration: 1260 divided by 100.
Set the pump to 12.6 millilitres per hour.
Check it: 12.6 times 100 gives back 1260 units an hour.

answer.q: Why does a patient in diabetic ketoacidosis breathe fast and deep?

els.title: title | DKA: breathing out acid
els.breath: flow 800 200 900 70 c=sky n=3 dots=1 | Fast, deep breaths
els.lbl: label 640 450 c=blue s=22 | Less CO2 = less acid
els.kuss: label 560 505 c=red s=26 | Kussmaul breathing: the body's acid alarm

steps.say: In diabetic ketoacidosis there's too little insulin, so sugar can't get into the cells.
The starving cells burn fat instead, and that makes ketones, which are acids.
The acid spills into the blood, and blood pH drops below its normal seven point four.
Carbon dioxide also makes acid in the blood, and the lungs can get rid of it.
So the brain drives fast, deep breaths that blow off carbon dioxide and pull the pH back up.
This is Kussmaul breathing, and it often smells fruity from the ketones.

answer.q: Find the highest and lowest points of f(x) = x^3 - 3x on [-2, 2].

els.title: title | Highest & lowest of x³ − 3x on [−2, 2]
els.t2: text 580 222 s=24 | 2. Check those, plus the ends ±2:
els.max: tag 760 380 330 44 s=22 f=#ffe0b2 | Highest: 2  (at x = −1 and 2)
els.min: tag 760 440 330 44 s=22 f=#d6ecff | Lowest: −2  (at x = −2 and 1)
els.final: text 580 510 s=22 | Check flat spots AND endpoints!

steps.say: We want the highest and lowest values of x cubed minus three x, but only from minus two to two.
These extremes hide where the curve goes flat, or at the ends of the interval.
The slope is f prime, three x squared minus three. Set it to zero: x is one or minus one.
Now plug in the flat spots and both ends. We get minus two, two, minus two, and two.
So the highest value is two, at x equals minus one and two. The lowest is minus two, at minus two and one.
Always check the endpoints too. Here they tie with the turning points!

answer.q: A ball is thrown at 20 m/s at 30 degrees above the ground. How far does it go?

els.title: title | How far does the ball fly?

steps.say: The ball leaves at twenty metres per second, tilted thirty degrees up.
Split that speed in two: about seventeen point three sideways, and ten metres per second upward.
Gravity cuts the upward ten by nine point eight each second, so it rises for about one second, then falls for one more.
Meanwhile, nothing slows it sideways, so it keeps going at seventeen point three the whole two seconds.
Distance is speed times time: seventeen point three times two point oh four.
So the ball lands about thirty five metres away.

answer.q: Why does adding salt raise water's boiling point?

els.title: title | Salt raises the boiling point
els.t102: label 60 108 c=red s=24 | Salty water: about 102 °C
els.zhead: label 480 108 s=24 | Zoomed in: the surface
els.legend: label 480 470 s=22 | blue = water    orange = salt ions

steps.say: Pure water boils at one hundred degrees Celsius.
Zoom in on the surface. Boiling means water molecules escape into the air as vapour.
do: fill m1 m3 m4 m6 m7 b1 b2 b3 b4 b5 b6 b7 b8 b9 b10

steps.say: Now add salt. It splits into ions that spread through the water, and some sit right at the surface.
do: fill i1 i2 i3 i4 i5 i6

steps.say: The ions take up surface spots and hold on to nearby water, so fewer molecules escape each second.
To get enough molecules out, the water needs extra energy, so it must get hotter before it boils.
More salt means a higher boiling point, but a pinch in pasta water changes it only a tiny bit.

answer.q: How does the electron transport chain make ATP?

els.title: title | Electron transport chain
els.total: text 250 75 s=26 | about 30 ATP from each glucose!

steps.say: Inside your mitochondria, a folded inner membrane works like a power station.
NADH from food hands over electrons, which pass along a chain of proteins.
The electrons' energy pumps hydrogen ions up across the membrane.
At the end, oxygen catches the tired electrons and becomes water.
Ions pile up on one side, like water behind a dam.
They rush back through ATP synthase, spinning it like a turbine, and each turn makes ATP.
So food energy becomes an ion flow, and that flow builds about thirty ATP per glucose.

answer.q: What does a p-value of 0.03 actually mean?

els.title: title | What a p-value of 0.03 means
els.curve: normal 70 130 560 300 mean=0 sd=1 from=1.88 to=4 | Results if the drug does nothing
els.l1: label 660 160 c=blue s=24 | Assume: no real effect
els.l2: label 660 225 c=red s=24 | Area in tail = 0.03
els.l3: label 660 265 c=red s=22 | 3 in 100 by chance alone
els.myth: callout 655 315 285 115 tip=600,400 k=thought | NOT a 3% chance the drug is useless

steps.say: A p-value answers one question: if nothing real were going on, how surprising would my data be?
Say you test a new drug. Imagine it does nothing at all. This curve shows the results luck alone would give.
Now your real result comes in, and it lands far out here, in the tail.
The shaded area past it is 0.03. If the drug did nothing, results this extreme would show up only about 3 times in 100.
It does not mean there's a 3 percent chance the drug is useless, or a 97 percent chance it works.
It only measures surprise. Below the usual 0.05 cut-off, we call the result statistically significant.

answer.q: How does the Fed raising interest rates lower inflation?

els.title: title | Higher rates, cooler prices
els.loans: tag 430 210 180 64 s=24 f=#ffe08a | Loans cost more
els.prob: tag 250 445 220 56 s=24 f=#ffd6d0 | Prices rising fast!
els.final: label 520 520 c=blue s=24 | Slower spending = slower price rises

steps.say: Inflation is when prices rise fast, often because everyone wants to buy more than shops can supply.
So the Fed raises its interest rate, and that pushes up rates across the economy.
Now loans for homes, cars and businesses cost more, and saving pays better.
So people borrow less and spend less, and more money sits in the bank instead.
With less spending, demand falls, and shops can't keep raising prices so easily.
Prices rise more slowly, and inflation cools down. The trade-off is slower growth for a while.
Deep under your feet, the Earth is so hot that some rock melts into a glowing liquid called magma.
do: flow dot 480,330 480,130 n=5 c=#ffb347 size=10 wobble=20

steps.say: The ground is cracked into giant plates, and where they pull apart or push together, magma finds a way up.
do: flow dot 480,560 480,300 n=5 c=#ff9a3a size=12 wobble=15

steps.say: Magma is lighter than the rock around it, so it rises and collects in a chamber under a mountain.
do: flow dot 480,560 480,470 n=5 c=#ffb347 size=11 at=1

steps.say: Gases trapped in the magma form bubbles that grow and push, so the pressure builds and builds.
do: flow dot 380,470 380,190 n=6 c=#ffe0b0 size=14 wobble=30
flow dot 560,470 560,190 n=6 c=#ffe0b0 size=18 wobble=30

steps.say: When the rock above can't hold any longer, it bursts open, blasting out lava, ash and gas.
The lava flows downhill, cools and hardens into new rock, and the volcano grows a little taller.
Every night you spend hours asleep, but your body is far from switched off.
Your brain replays the day and stores what you learned as lasting memories.
do: flow dot 40,120 400,280 n=6 c=#f6d65a once gap=.5 spread=60
flow dot 920,480 560,320 n=6 c=#f6d65a once gap=.5 spread=60 at=.8

steps.say: It also washes away the waste that builds up while you are awake.
Meanwhile your body repairs itself, mending muscles and helping you grow.
Sleep gives your defences strength too, so white blood cells can fight germs.
So after a good night's sleep, you wake up sharper, healthier and ready to go.

answer.q: How does the internet reach my phone?

steps.say: When you open a video, your phone sends out a tiny request, like a note asking for it.
do: flow dot 360,280 900,200 n=5 c=#ffd36b size=10 speed=.5

steps.say: That video lives on powerful computers called servers, often in another country.
The data races as flashes of light through glass cables under the ground and sea.
It arrives at a phone mast or the router in your home.
From there, invisible radio waves carry it through the air to your phone.
do: flow dot 330,270 600,320 n=6 c=#ffd36b size=9 wobble=20

steps.say: Requests go out and answers come back, round the world, in less than a second.
Water on Earth is always on the move, in a giant loop called the water cycle.
The sun warms the sea, and water rises into the air as invisible vapour. That is evaporation.
High up, the vapour cools into tiny droplets that gather into clouds. That is condensation.
When the droplets get heavy, they fall as rain or snow. That is precipitation.
Rivers carry the water back to the sea, and the whole cycle starts again.
Honey starts in flowers, as a sweet, sugary juice called nectar.
A bee sips the nectar and carries it home in a special honey stomach.
At the hive, she passes it from mouth to mouth to other bees, who add enzymes that break the sugar down.
They spread it into wax cells and fan their wings to dry the water out.
When the honey is thick, they seal each cell with a wax lid.
Sealed honey keeps for months, and it feeds the hive all winter.
A plane weighs as much as a big herd of elephants, so how does it stay up in the sky?
First, the engines push air backwards very hard, and that pushes the plane forwards.
do: flow dot 430,320 20,320 n=10 c=#ffffff speed=1.2 fade
line 700,230 880,230 c=#f6d65a lw=8 arrow draw at=.5

steps.say: As the plane speeds along, air rushes over and under the curved, tilted wings.
The wings bend the air downwards, and the air pushes back by lifting the wings upwards.
do: line 490,250 490,70 c=#7cf08a lw=10 arrow draw at=1

steps.say: Lift beats the plane's weight, thrust beats the drag of the air, and the plane flies.
do: line 480,360 480,530 c=#f07a7a lw=9 arrow draw at=.6
line 600,300 800,300 c=#f6d65a lw=9 arrow draw at=1.2
line 360,300 160,300 c=#c9cde6 lw=9 arrow draw at=1.8

steps.say: That's why planes race down a long runway. Once they're fast enough, the wings lift them into the sky.
Earth is wrapped in a thin blanket of air that keeps it warm enough for life.
When we burn coal, oil and gas in factories and cars, we release carbon dioxide.
do: flow co2 280,260 380,-20 n=6 speed=.4 fade wobble=40
flow co2 600,470 700,-20 n=4 speed=.3 fade wobble=40

steps.say: That gas thickens the blanket, so more of the sun's heat gets trapped.
Slowly, the whole planet grows warmer.
Ice melts, seas rise, and storms, floods and heatwaves grow stronger.
That long-term shift in Earth's weather is climate change. Cleaner energy and more trees can help slow it.
do: flow co2 1000,120 480,380 n=6 once gap=.4 spread=120

steps.say: A battery is a little box of stored chemical energy, waiting to become electricity.
Inside are two different ends, a negative one and a positive one, with a chemical paste between them.
Chemical reactions pile up tiny electrons at the negative end, eager to escape.
Connect a wire, and the electrons rush through it to the positive end, lighting a bulb on the way.
Inside, the paste carries charged particles across to balance things, so the flow keeps going.
When the chemicals are used up, the battery goes flat. A charger pushes them back so it can work again.

objects.say: Long ago, talking drums sent messages from village to village.
Then the telegraph tapped out dots and dashes along a wire.
The telephone let people hear each other's voices from far away.
In the nineteen eighties, the first mobile phones were as big as bricks.
Today, a smartphone in your pocket can call, text, and see the whole world.
And now, even a watch on your wrist can take a call.
Long ago, people pushed and pulled heavy wooden carts by hand.
Then horses pulled carriages on big spoked wheels.
Around 1900, engines replaced horses, and the first cars rattled along.
Later, cars grew lower and faster, with closed roofs and big windows.
Today, many cars glide quietly, powered by electricity from a battery.
Long ago, people told the time from a shadow on a stone sundial.
An hourglass measured time with falling sand.
Pendulum clocks swung back and forth to tick steady seconds.
A pocket watch let people carry the time with them.
Wristwatches strapped the time right onto your arm.
And today, a smartwatch shows the time, your steps, and your messages.

answer.q: How did we store information over time?

objects.say: Long ago, people pressed wedge marks into wet clay tablets to keep records.
Later, words were written on long scrolls of papyrus, rolled up for safekeeping.
Books bound many pages together, so you could flip straight to any part.
Computers saved files on floppy disks, holding about one book's worth of text.
A tiny USB stick could later carry thousands of books in your pocket.
And today, much of our information lives in the cloud, on distant computers.
Long ago, people cooked food in a pot over an open wood fire.
Later, they baked bread inside domed clay ovens.
Iron wood stoves kept the fire safely shut inside a metal box.
Gas cookers brought quick blue flames you could turn up or down.
Microwave ovens heat food in minutes using invisible waves.
And today, induction hobs heat the pan itself, with no flame at all.
Long before people flew, birds showed how wings could ride the air.
In 1783, a hot-air balloon lifted people into the sky for the first time.
In 1903, the Wright brothers flew the first powered airplane, a biplane.
By the 1930s, propeller airliners carried passengers between cities.
Jet engines then made planes much faster, flying high above the clouds.
And today, rockets carry people beyond the sky, into space.
Before bulbs, people lit their homes with wax candles.
Oil lamps burned brighter, with a glass chimney around the flame.
Then the electric bulb made a thin wire filament glow.
But those bulbs wasted most of their power as heat.
Fluorescent tubes made gas glow, using far less energy.
Today, LED bulbs give bright light and last for many years.
Long ago, people traded with shiny cowrie shells instead of money.
Then metal coins were stamped, so everyone could trust their value.
Paper banknotes were lighter, and stood for gold kept safe in a bank.
Plastic bank cards let people pay without carrying cash at all.
And today, a phone can pay with a single tap.

els.title: title | How a cloud forms
els.t3: tag 475 100 170 40 s=18 | 3. Air cools up high
els.tempL: label 615 330 c=blue s=22 | colder higher up

steps.say: Step 1: The sun warms oceans, lakes and puddles.
Step 2: Some water evaporates, turning into invisible vapour that rises with warm air.
Step 3: The higher the air goes, the colder it gets.
Step 4: Cold vapour condenses into tiny droplets, each one forming around a speck of dust.
Step 5: Billions of these droplets crowd together, and we see them as a cloud!

answer.q: [numbered] How does a car engine start?

els.title: title | How a car engine starts

steps.say: Step 1: You turn the key or press start, which closes an electric circuit.
Step 2: The battery sends a big rush of current to the starter.
Step 3: The starter, a small electric motor, begins to spin.
Step 4: Its gear grabs the flywheel and cranks the engine round.
Step 5: Pistons move, sucking in fuel and air, and a spark makes it burn and push down.
Step 6: Now each burn turns the engine, so the starter lets go and it runs by itself.

answer.q: [numbered] A patient weighs 70 kg. Heparin is ordered at 18 units/kg/hr, and the bag has 25,000 units in 250 mL. What rate in mL/hr?

els.t1: tag 160 75 230 40 s=20 f=#e3f2fd | 1. Dose per hour
els.t4: tag 200 495 220 40 s=20 f=#e3f2fd | 4. Set the pump

steps.say: Step 1: Multiply weight by dose: 70 kilograms times 18 units is 1,260 units every hour.
Step 2: Find the bag's strength: 25,000 units in 250 millilitres is 100 units per millilitre.
Step 3: Divide the hourly dose by the strength: 1,260 divided by 100 gives 12.6.
Step 4: Set the pump to 12.6 millilitres per hour. Units over units cancel, leaving millilitres per hour.

els.tag5: tag 860 40 160 40 s=18 f=#fff3c4 | 5. Millions of drops

steps.say: Step 1: A rainbow needs two things: sunlight, and raindrops in the air.
Step 2: Sunlight looks white, but it is really a mix of every colour.
Step 3: When light enters a raindrop it bends, and each colour bends by a different amount.
Step 4: The colours bounce off the back of the drop and come out spread into a fan.
Step 5: Millions of drops do this together, so with the sun behind you, you see a giant arc of colour.

answer.q: How does a VR headset work?

steps.say: Step 1: Inside the headset, one screen sits just inches from your face, showing two pictures, one for each eye.
Step 2: Your eyes can't focus that close, so lenses bend the light and make the screen look far away.
Step 3: Each picture is drawn from a slightly different angle, and your brain blends them into one 3D scene.
Step 4: Motion sensors, like a gyroscope, feel every turn of your head.
Step 5: The headset redraws your view about ninety times a second, so the world moves with you and feels real.

els.title: title | How a leaf makes food
els.co2: flow 60 400 300 335 c=sky n=2 dots=1 | Carbon dioxide

steps.say: Step 1: Plants make their own food, and the leaf is their kitchen.
Step 2: Sunlight hits the leaf and gives it energy.
Step 3: Water travels up from the roots into the leaf.
Step 4: Carbon dioxide comes in from the air through tiny holes.
Step 5: Using the sun's energy, the leaf turns water and carbon dioxide into sugar, its food.
Step 6: Then it lets out oxygen, the very air we breathe. That process is called photosynthesis.

answer.q: Why do we have day and night?

steps.say: Step 1: The Sun shines its light toward the Earth all the time.
Step 2: Earth is a ball, so only the half facing the Sun is lit. That half has day.
Step 3: Earth is always spinning, like a top, so places keep turning around.
Step 4: When your place turns away from the Sun, it falls into shadow, and it is night.
Step 5: One full spin takes twenty-four hours, so you get day, then night, again and again.

els.cmp2: label 140 400 c=red s=28 | 23 < 38, so throw away the right side
els.fnd: label 500 340 c=green s=26 | Found in 3 checks!
els.sum: label 140 470 c=blue s=28 | Each check halves the list: 1 million items take about 20 checks

steps.say: Binary search finds an item in a sorted list by cutting the list in half again and again.
do: fill c0 c1 c2 c3 c4 c5 c6 c7 c8

steps.say: Say we want to find twenty three. We start by looking at the middle item, sixteen.
Twenty three is bigger than sixteen, so it can't be anywhere on the left. We throw that whole half away.
Now we check the middle of what's left, which is thirty eight. That's too big, so we drop the right side.
Only one item is left, and it's twenty three. Found it in just three checks.
Every check halves the list, so even a million items take only about twenty checks.

answer.q: What is the difference between mitosis and meiosis?

els.title: title | Mitosis vs meiosis
els.nme: label 580 500 s=22 | 4 unique cells, half the set

steps.say: Mitosis and meiosis are the two ways a cell can divide.
In mitosis, one cell copies its forty six chromosomes, then splits in two.
The two new cells are identical copies, used to grow and repair your body.
Meiosis divides twice, making four cells, and halves the chromosomes to twenty three.
Each one is unique because the genes get shuffled. These become eggs or sperm.
So mitosis makes copies of you, and meiosis makes new mixes for the next generation.

els.title: title | Interest on interest
els.chart: moneygrow 350 90 570 350 p=100 r=10 n=10 cur=$ simple=1 | Compound vs simple
els.note: label 400 525 c=red s=22 | After 10 years: about $259, not $200

steps.say: Compound interest means you earn interest on your interest, not just on what you put in.
Say you save one hundred dollars at ten percent a year.
After one year the bank adds ten dollars, so you have one hundred and ten.
Next year, ten percent of one hundred and ten is eleven dollars. The interest earned interest too.
Each year the pile is bigger, so each year's interest is bigger, and the growth speeds up.
After ten years you'd have about two hundred fifty nine dollars, not two hundred. So start saving early!

answer.q: A patient weighs 70 kg. Heparin is ordered at 18 units/kg/hr, and the bag has 25,000 units in 250 mL. What rate in mL/hr?

els.title: title | Heparin drip rate
els.check: label 60 470 c=red s=20 | Check: 12.6 mL × 100 = 1260 units/hr ✓

steps.say: First, find the hourly dose. Multiply the weight by the ordered dose.
Seventy kilograms times eighteen units is 1260 units per hour.
Next, find the concentration: 25,000 units divided by 250 millilitres is 100 units per millilitre.
Now divide the dose by the concentration: 1260 divided by 100.
Set the pump to 12.6 millilitres per hour.
Check it: 12.6 times 100 gives back 1260 units an hour.

answer.q: Why does a patient in diabetic ketoacidosis breathe fast and deep?

els.title: title | DKA: breathing out acid
els.breath: flow 800 200 900 70 c=sky n=3 dots=1 | Fast, deep breaths
els.lbl: label 640 450 c=blue s=22 | Less CO2 = less acid
els.kuss: label 560 505 c=red s=26 | Kussmaul breathing: the body's acid alarm

steps.say: In diabetic ketoacidosis there's too little insulin, so sugar can't get into the cells.
The starving cells burn fat instead, and that makes ketones, which are acids.
The acid spills into the blood, and blood pH drops below its normal seven point four.
Carbon dioxide also makes acid in the blood, and the lungs can get rid of it.
So the brain drives fast, deep breaths that blow off carbon dioxide and pull the pH back up.
This is Kussmaul breathing, and it often smells fruity from the ketones.

answer.q: Find the highest and lowest points of f(x) = x^3 - 3x on [-2, 2].

els.title: title | Highest & lowest of x³ − 3x on [−2, 2]
els.t2: text 580 222 s=24 | 2. Check those, plus the ends ±2:
els.max: tag 760 380 330 44 s=22 f=#ffe0b2 | Highest: 2  (at x = −1 and 2)
els.min: tag 760 440 330 44 s=22 f=#d6ecff | Lowest: −2  (at x = −2 and 1)
els.final: text 580 510 s=22 | Check flat spots AND endpoints!

steps.say: We want the highest and lowest values of x cubed minus three x, but only from minus two to two.
These extremes hide where the curve goes flat, or at the ends of the interval.
The slope is f prime, three x squared minus three. Set it to zero: x is one or minus one.
Now plug in the flat spots and both ends. We get minus two, two, minus two, and two.
So the highest value is two, at x equals minus one and two. The lowest is minus two, at minus two and one.
Always check the endpoints too. Here they tie with the turning points!

answer.q: A ball is thrown at 20 m/s at 30 degrees above the ground. How far does it go?

els.title: title | How far does the ball fly?

steps.say: The ball leaves at twenty metres per second, tilted thirty degrees up.
Split that speed in two: about seventeen point three sideways, and ten metres per second upward.
Gravity cuts the upward ten by nine point eight each second, so it rises for about one second, then falls for one more.
Meanwhile, nothing slows it sideways, so it keeps going at seventeen point three the whole two seconds.
Distance is speed times time: seventeen point three times two point oh four.
So the ball lands about thirty five metres away.

answer.q: Why does adding salt raise water's boiling point?

els.title: title | Salt raises the boiling point
els.t102: label 60 108 c=red s=24 | Salty water: about 102 °C
els.zhead: label 480 108 s=24 | Zoomed in: the surface
els.legend: label 480 470 s=22 | blue = water    orange = salt ions

steps.say: Pure water boils at one hundred degrees Celsius.
Zoom in on the surface. Boiling means water molecules escape into the air as vapour.
do: fill m1 m3 m4 m6 m7 b1 b2 b3 b4 b5 b6 b7 b8 b9 b10

steps.say: Now add salt. It splits into ions that spread through the water, and some sit right at the surface.
do: fill i1 i2 i3 i4 i5 i6

steps.say: The ions take up surface spots and hold on to nearby water, so fewer molecules escape each second.
To get enough molecules out, the water needs extra energy, so it must get hotter before it boils.
More salt means a higher boiling point, but a pinch in pasta water changes it only a tiny bit.

answer.q: How does the electron transport chain make ATP?

els.title: title | Electron transport chain
els.total: text 250 75 s=26 | about 30 ATP from each glucose!

steps.say: Inside your mitochondria, a folded inner membrane works like a power station.
NADH from food hands over electrons, which pass along a chain of proteins.
The electrons' energy pumps hydrogen ions up across the membrane.
At the end, oxygen catches the tired electrons and becomes water.
Ions pile up on one side, like water behind a dam.
They rush back through ATP synthase, spinning it like a turbine, and each turn makes ATP.
So food energy becomes an ion flow, and that flow builds about thirty ATP per glucose.

answer.q: What does a p-value of 0.03 actually mean?

els.title: title | What a p-value of 0.03 means
els.curve: normal 70 130 560 300 mean=0 sd=1 from=1.88 to=4 | Results if the drug does nothing
els.l1: label 660 160 c=blue s=24 | Assume: no real effect
els.l2: label 660 225 c=red s=24 | Area in tail = 0.03
els.l3: label 660 265 c=red s=22 | 3 in 100 by chance alone
els.myth: callout 655 315 285 115 tip=600,400 k=thought | NOT a 3% chance the drug is useless

steps.say: A p-value answers one question: if nothing real were going on, how surprising would my data be?
Say you test a new drug. Imagine it does nothing at all. This curve shows the results luck alone would give.
Now your real result comes in, and it lands far out here, in the tail.
The shaded area past it is 0.03. If the drug did nothing, results this extreme would show up only about 3 times in 100.
It does not mean there's a 3 percent chance the drug is useless, or a 97 percent chance it works.
It only measures surprise. Below the usual 0.05 cut-off, we call the result statistically significant.

answer.q: How does the Fed raising interest rates lower inflation?

els.title: title | Higher rates, cooler prices
els.loans: tag 430 210 180 64 s=24 f=#ffe08a | Loans cost more
els.prob: tag 250 445 220 56 s=24 f=#ffd6d0 | Prices rising fast!
els.final: label 520 520 c=blue s=24 | Slower spending = slower price rises

steps.say: Inflation is when prices rise fast, often because everyone wants to buy more than shops can supply.
So the Fed raises its interest rate, and that pushes up rates across the economy.
Now loans for homes, cars and businesses cost more, and saving pays better.
So people borrow less and spend less, and more money sits in the bank instead.
With less spending, demand falls, and shops can't keep raising prices so easily.
Prices rise more slowly, and inflation cools down. The trade-off is slower growth for a while.

Water on Earth is always on the move, in a giant loop called the water cycle.
The sun warms the sea, and water rises into the air as invisible vapour. That is evaporation.
High up, the vapour cools into tiny droplets that gather into clouds. That is condensation.
When the droplets get heavy, they fall as rain or snow. That is precipitation.
Rivers carry the water back to the sea, and the whole cycle starts again.
Honey starts in flowers, as a sweet, sugary juice called nectar.
A bee sips the nectar and carries it home in a special honey stomach.
At the hive, she passes it from mouth to mouth to other bees, who add enzymes that break the sugar down.
They spread it into wax cells and fan their wings to dry the water out.
When the honey is thick, they seal each cell with a wax lid.
Sealed honey keeps for months, and it feeds the hive all winter.

Ice melts, seas rise, and storms, floods and heatwaves grow stronger.
That long-term shift in Earth's weather is climate change. Cleaner energy and more trees can help slow it.

steps.say: A battery is a little box of stored chemical energy, waiting to become electricity.
Inside are two different ends, a negative one and a positive one, with a chemical paste between them.
Chemical reactions pile up tiny electrons at the negative end, eager to escape.
Connect a wire, and the electrons rush through it to the positive end, lighting a bulb on the way.
Inside, the paste carries charged particles across to balance things, so the flow keeps going.
When the chemicals are used up, the battery goes flat. A charger pushes them back so it can work again.

objects.say: Long ago, talking drums sent messages from village to village.
Then the telegraph tapped out dots and dashes along a wire.
The telephone let people hear each other's voices from far away.
In the nineteen eighties, the first mobile phones were as big as bricks.
Today, a smartphone in your pocket can call, text, and see the whole world.
And now, even a watch on your wrist can take a call.
Long ago, people pushed and pulled heavy wooden carts by hand.
Then horses pulled carriages on big spoked wheels.
Around 1900, engines replaced horses, and the first cars rattled along.
Later, cars grew lower and faster, with closed roofs and big windows.
Today, many cars glide quietly, powered by electricity from a battery.
Long ago, people told the time from a shadow on a stone sundial.
An hourglass measured time with falling sand.
Pendulum clocks swung back and forth to tick steady seconds.
A pocket watch let people carry the time with them.
Wristwatches strapped the time right onto your arm.
And today, a smartwatch shows the time, your steps, and your messages.

answer.q: How did we store information over time?

objects.say: Long ago, people pressed wedge marks into wet clay tablets to keep records.
Later, words were written on long scrolls of papyrus, rolled up for safekeeping.
Books bound many pages together, so you could flip straight to any part.
Computers saved files on floppy disks, holding about one book's worth of text.
A tiny USB stick could later carry thousands of books in your pocket.
And today, much of our information lives in the cloud, on distant computers.
Long ago, people cooked food in a pot over an open wood fire.
Later, they baked bread inside domed clay ovens.
Iron wood stoves kept the fire safely shut inside a metal box.
Gas cookers brought quick blue flames you could turn up or down.
Microwave ovens heat food in minutes using invisible waves.
And today, induction hobs heat the pan itself, with no flame at all.
Long before people flew, birds showed how wings could ride the air.
In 1783, a hot-air balloon lifted people into the sky for the first time.
In 1903, the Wright brothers flew the first powered airplane, a biplane.
By the 1930s, propeller airliners carried passengers between cities.
Jet engines then made planes much faster, flying high above the clouds.
And today, rockets carry people beyond the sky, into space.
Before bulbs, people lit their homes with wax candles.
Oil lamps burned brighter, with a glass chimney around the flame.
Then the electric bulb made a thin wire filament glow.
But those bulbs wasted most of their power as heat.
Fluorescent tubes made gas glow, using far less energy.
Today, LED bulbs give bright light and last for many years.
Long ago, people traded with shiny cowrie shells instead of money.
Then metal coins were stamped, so everyone could trust their value.
Paper banknotes were lighter, and stood for gold kept safe in a bank.
Plastic bank cards let people pay without carrying cash at all.
And today, a phone can pay with a single tap.

answer.q: Why do we have day and night?

steps.say: Step 1: The Sun shines its light toward the Earth all the time.
Step 2: Earth is a ball, so only the half facing the Sun is lit. That half has day.
Step 3: Earth is always spinning, like a top, so places keep turning around.
Step 4: When your place turns away from the Sun, it falls into shadow, and it is night.
Step 5: One full spin takes twenty-four hours, so you get day, then night, again and again.

answer.q: How does the engine of a car start?

els.title: title | Starting a car engine
els.spark: label 640 130 c=red s=24 | spark + fuel = bang!
els.done: label 250 515 c=blue s=26 | Now the engine runs itself, and the starter lets go

steps.say: When you turn the key or press start, you close an electric switch.
That lets the battery send a big burst of current to a small electric motor, called the starter.
The starter spins a heavy wheel, the flywheel, which turns the engine's crankshaft.
Now the pistons move, sucking in air and fuel and squeezing it tight.
A spark plug fires, the fuel explodes, and the blast pushes the piston down hard.
Each bang keeps the crankshaft turning, so the engine runs by itself and the starter switches off.

answer.q: How does a car's engine work?

els.title: title | Inside a car engine
els.note: label 560 515 c=blue s=24 | Thousands of bangs a minute!

steps.say: A car engine turns fuel into motion, using lots of tiny explosions.
First, the piston slides down and sucks fuel and air into the cylinder.
Then it moves back up and squeezes that mixture tight.
A spark plug lights it, and the bang shoves the piston down hard.
Finally the piston rises again and pushes the burnt gas out the exhaust.
The rod turns a crankshaft, and gears pass that spin to the wheels.
Suck, squeeze, bang, blow, thousands of times a minute, and the car rolls on.
